"""Decrypt a case archive.

The archives are AES-256 zips, which `zipfile` cannot read. The starter script
shells out to 7z; we use `pyzipper` instead, for three reasons:

* No external install. 7z is a per-machine dependency that will bite exactly one
  teammate at exactly the wrong moment.
* No subprocess in the 60-second window - process spawn plus disk round-trip,
  gone.
* We can extract straight to memory. Nothing needs to touch the filesystem
  before the model sees it, though we also write it out for the audit trail.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import logging
from pathlib import Path

import pyzipper

log = logging.getLogger(__name__)

#: A case is three or four small files; anything larger is not a case.
MAX_MEMBER_BYTES: int = 32 * 1024 * 1024


class DecryptError(RuntimeError):
    """The archive could not be opened with the given key."""


def archive_path(cases_dir: str | Path, game_id: int) -> Path:
    return Path(cases_dir) / f"case_{game_id:02d}.zip"


def read_members(archive: str | Path, key: str) -> dict[str, bytes]:
    """Every member of the archive, in memory.

    Raises `DecryptError` rather than leaking pyzipper's exception types, so the
    orchestrator has one thing to catch.
    """
    path = Path(archive)
    if not path.exists():
        raise DecryptError(f"missing {path} - stage the archives before the round")

    try:
        with pyzipper.AESZipFile(path) as zip_file:
            zip_file.setpassword(key.encode())
            out: dict[str, bytes] = {}
            for info in zip_file.infolist():
                if info.is_dir():
                    continue
                if info.file_size > MAX_MEMBER_BYTES:
                    log.warning("c2f skipping oversized member %s", info.filename)
                    continue
                # Flatten any directory nesting; case layouts are flat.
                out[Path(info.filename).name] = zip_file.read(info)
    except Exception as error:  # noqa: BLE001 - one failure type for the caller
        raise DecryptError(f"could not decrypt {path.name}: {error}") from error

    if not out:
        raise DecryptError(f"{path.name} decrypted to nothing")
    return out


def extract_case(archive: str | Path, key: str, out_dir: str | Path) -> Path:
    """Decrypt and write the files out. Returns the directory written to.

    We still write to disk even though parsing could work from memory: a round
    that scores oddly is much easier to explain when the exact inputs are
    sitting on disk next to the decision log.
    """
    members = read_members(archive, key)
    directory = Path(out_dir)
    directory.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    for name, data in members.items():
        (directory / name).write_bytes(data)
    return directory

content.text:
## What the model actually receives

Exactly one user message per call, ~1,850 chars for case 0 — shown in full above. Three calls get **the same** user message; only the system prompt differs. The user message has three blocks:

1. `=== INSURANCE POLICY ===` — `policy.txt`, verbatim
2. `=== DAMAGE DESCRIPTION ===` — `description.txt`, verbatim
3. `=== INVOICE LINE ITEMS (1) ===` — one rendered line per parsed row, plus a count assertion

Built by [`case_context`](backend/app/c2f/inference/prompts.py#L111). The invoice line format is `- item_id=1 | quantity=1 unit | New Bike`, from [`render_items`](backend/app/c2f/inference/prompts.py#L100).

## How policy and description are handled

They are **not parsed**. [`load_case`](backend/app/c2f/parsing/case.py#L31) reads them as raw UTF-8 and passes the bytes through untouched — no clause splitting, no section extraction, no summarisation. Files are matched by filename *stem*, not exact name:

| match on stem | lands in |
|---|---|
| contains `polic` or `bedingung` | `bundle.policy` |
| contains `descr`, `damage`, `beschreib`, `schaden` | `bundle.description` |
| any other `.txt`/`.md`, if description still empty | `bundle.description` |
| `.pdf` (prefers a stem containing `invoice`) | parsed as the invoice |
| `.png/.jpg/.jpeg/.webp/.gif` | `bundle.image_paths` |

Deliberate: clause extraction would be a lossy pre-filter in front of the model, and case 0 shows why that's dangerous — the decisive sentence is §4's "market value at the time of the theft", which a naive extractor tuned for exclusions would drop. Two limits: text is truncated at 40,000 chars (`MAX_TEXT_CHARS`), and `errors="replace"` means bad encoding degrades to a replacement char rather than raising.

**`image_paths` is collected but never sent.** Case 0 has no images, so this is untested and currently a gap — cases that ship `images.png` will silently ignore it.

## The invoice is the only thing parsed

[`extract_text`](backend/app/c2f/parsing/invoice.py#L67) pulls the pypdf text layer, then [`parse_line_items`](backend/app/c2f/parsing/invoice.py#L79) walks it as a state machine: start collecting after a `POS. DESCRIPTION` header, stop at a footer (`Created on`, `Page N`, `Subtotal`, …), skip column-header noise.

Each row is matched right-to-left — `^(\d{1,3})[.)]?\s+(.+?)\s+([\d.,]+)\s*([A-Za-z%]{0,12})\s*$` — with a greedy description so the **last** number on the line is the quantity. That's what stops "26 inch wheel" from parsing 26 as the quantity. Rows with no quantity column fall back to `1.0`. `POS` becomes both `item_id` and `index`, and `index` is what the submission API keys on, so it's never renumbered.

## Flow, extraction to decision

```
case_NN.zip  ──pyzipper AES──▶  policy.txt  description.txt  invoices.pdf
                                    │            │              │
                                 verbatim     verbatim      pypdf text
                                    │            │              │
                                    └────────────┴──────────────┴──▶ CaseBundle
                                                                        │
                    ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                    ▼  one user message, three system prompts, asyncio.gather
        ┌───────────┴───────────┬───────────────────┐
     validity                pricing             skeptic          ← 25s deadline each
     p_valid                 q10..q90            multiplier
        └───────────┬───────────┴───────────────────┘
                    ▼  extract_json → index_by_item → merge_inferences
              list[ItemInference]        (one per parsed row, always)
                    │
                    ▼  FairValueDistribution.from_inference
        unit ladder × quantity × skeptic(clamped 0.5–1.0) × calibration
                    │
                    ▼  S(a) = p_valid · (1 − F₊(a))
                    │
                    ▼  decide()
          a = argmax a·S(a)          b = Q(1 − ⅔/p_valid), or 0 if p_valid < ⅔
                    │
                    ▼  guardrails.check → repair → build_payload → PUT
```

Three things worth knowing about that middle section:

**The quantity multiply happens in code, not in a prompt.** The pricing prompt is told to price *one unit* and ignore quantity entirely; `from_inference` multiplies. The guardrail then verifies the derivation (`q50_gross == quantity × unit_q50 × skeptic × mu_shift`), which is what catches a skipped or doubled multiply at any quantity.

**Every parsed row always gets an `ItemInference`.** [`merge_inferences`](backend/app/c2f/inference/schemas.py#L131) fills gaps rather than dropping items — if pricing returns nothing for row 2, that row gets a wide fallback ladder and `degraded=True`, but it still reaches the payload. Omitting a line doesn't opt us out of it; the server just defaults it to `0/0`, which collects nothing and pays the 1.5× penalty on every fair charge.

**Failures degrade per call and per item, never per round.** A timeout, a transport error, a refusal (HTTP 200 with `stop_reason="refusal"`), or unparseable JSON all resolve to an empty mapping for that one call, and the other two still merge.

**One thing that isn't wired yet**: the deadline in [`analyse_case`](backend/app/c2f/inference/analyse.py#L99) is per-call (25s), not anchored to a round clock — and there's no double-submit. So right now a slow round can consume 25s of inference with no safety-net submission already on the server. That's the orchestrator work, and it's the next thing I'd build.
What is the user message?

In the Messages API a request has two separate parts: a `system` parameter and a `messages` array. Our call passes exactly one message:

```python
completion = await provider.complete(
    [{"role": "user", "content": user}],   # ← the user message
    system=system,                          # ← the role instructions
    max_tokens=8_000,
)
```

[analyse.py:63](backend/app/c2f/inference/analyse.py#L63). So "the user message" is that single `content` string — the case data. The system prompt is what varies between the validity, pricing and skeptic calls; the user message is byte-identical across all three.

For case 0 it is 1,853 characters, assembled by [`case_context`](backend/app/c2f/inference/prompts.py#L111) as four blocks joined by blank lines:

```
=== INSURANCE POLICY ===
<all 1,495 chars of policy.txt, verbatim — including the ==== banner lines,
 numbered sections 1–6, and "END OF DOCUMENT">

=== DAMAGE DESCRIPTION ===
Client came back from work, his mountain bike was stolen. The mountain bike was
firmly locked against a lamp post. When he came back, the bike was worth 420 Euros.

=== INVOICE LINE ITEMS (1) ===
- item_id=1 | quantity=1 unit | New Bike

Return exactly 1 objects, one per item_id above, in the same order.
```

The full untruncated version is in [my earlier output](#) — nothing was elided there.

Notes on the construction:

- The `===` block headers are ours; they exist so the model can tell where the policy stops and the damage report starts. The `====` rows *inside* the policy block are QuantCo's own formatting, passed through untouched.
- The `(1)` in the invoice header and the closing `Return exactly 1 objects` line are the same count, twice, on purpose — a dropped item is the most expensive parsing failure, so the count is asserted rather than implied. (The grammar is wrong for n=1; harmless, and I left it rather than branch on plurality.)
- `item_id=1` is the invoice's POS column. The model must echo it back, and it's the same value the submission API keys on as `index`.
- The policy block is skippable — `case_context(..., include_policy=False)` omits it. Nothing uses that now; the pricing call needed the policy, which is what the case 0 comparison showed.
What does the LLM do in our pipeline
It converts documents into numbers, and nothing else. Three calls, all semantic, none of them decides anything.

content.text:
## Its entire job: three numbers per line item

| Call | System prompt | Produces | Used as |
|---|---|---|---|
| `validity` | senior claims examiner | `p_valid` — P(covered **and** related) | scales the whole survival curve; sets `b = 0` when < ⅔ |
| `pricing` | claims assessor applying the basis of indemnity | `q10 q25 q50 q75 q90`, per **unit** | the shape of the price belief |
| `skeptic` | adversarial auditor | `suggested_multiplier` | shrink on the ladder, clamped to [0.5, 1.0] |

That's it. Everything downstream — the survival function, `argmax a·S(a)`, the ⅔ rule, the guardrails, the payload — is deterministic arithmetic over those numbers.

## Four things it is explicitly not allowed to do

**It never sees the payoff table.** No prompt mentions `a`, `b`, the ⅔ rule, the 1.5× penalty, or the cap. It answers "what do these documents imply", not "what should we bid". Telling it the incentives would invite it to skew the estimate toward the answer it thinks we want, and we'd lose the ability to check the estimate independently of the decision.

**It never multiplies.** The pricing prompt says *"Price ONE UNIT of the item, not the whole line. Ignore the quantity entirely."* `from_inference` does `unit × quantity` in code, and the guardrail re-derives it. A model that quietly returns a line total instead of a unit price gets caught rather than believed.

**It cannot veto an item.** The skeptic returns a multiplier, not a rejection, and it's clamped so it can only argue prices *down*, never up. A veto is a cliff; a shrink degrades.

**It cannot set `p_covered × p_related`.** `p_valid` is asked for jointly and read directly. The two marginals are collected for display and never multiplied — they're strongly dependent, so the product understates validity.

## How much its output is trusted: not much

Every value passes through coercion before it reaches the maths. `p_valid` of `96` is read as 0.96 (models emit percentages unprompted). A quantile ladder that's tied, inverted, zero, or contains `NaN` is forced monotone by `_sanitise`. A reply wrapped in prose or ```json fences is recovered by a string-aware brace scan. A call that times out, errors, refuses (HTTP 200 with `stop_reason="refusal"`), or returns unparseable JSON becomes an empty mapping — and the *other two calls still merge*. Any item the model drops gets a wide fallback ladder and `degraded=True`, but still reaches the payload.

So the LLM is a component that can fail in any way at any time, and the round still submits.

## Two honest caveats

**Six of the fields we ask for are never read.** `exclusion_hit`, `indemnity_basis`, `unit_basis`, `price_basis`, `inflation_flags`, `qty_plausible` — requested in the prompts, discarded by `merge_inferences`. They aren't useless: naming the indemnity clause before emitting a number is the reasoning step that makes the number right on case 0. But they should be persisted, because they're exactly the evidence the audit UI needs and the write-up's "here's why" panel. Right now that reasoning is generated and thrown away.

**The LLM has not actually run once.** `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is empty. Every number I've shown you — including the +1273 on case 0 — comes from beliefs I wrote by hand to stand in for what the model should produce. The entire semantic layer is tested only against a scripted fake provider. Whether Opus 5 reliably finds §4's market-value clause and collapses the spread to near-zero is the single biggest unverified assumption in the system, and it's the difference between +1273 and −161.

"""Pull line items out of `invoices.pdf`.

The submission API addresses line items by their 1-based `index`, which is the
POS column on the invoice. Getting that mapping wrong misprices every item in
the round, so the parser is deliberately literal: it trusts the POS column and
never renumbers.

Rows look like

    POS. DESCRIPTION            AMOUNT UNIT TOTAL
    1    New Bike                    1 unit

with TOTAL empty - the prices are the thing we are being asked for. Parsed
right-to-left, because a description may itself contain numbers ("26 inch
wheel") while the trailing `amount unit` pair is positionally reliable.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import logging
import re
from pathlib import Path

from app.c2f.models import LineItem

log = logging.getLogger(__name__)

#: `1  New Bike  1 unit`  ->  (pos, description, amount, unit)
#: The description is greedy so the LAST number on the row is the amount.
_ROW = re.compile(r"^(\d{1,3})[.)]?\s+(.+?)\s+([\d.,]+)\s*([A-Za-z%]{0,12})\s*$")
#: A row with no amount column at all. Quantity then defaults to 1.
_BARE_ROW = re.compile(r"^(\d{1,3})[.)]?\s+(.+?)\s*$")

_HEADER = re.compile(r"POS\.?\s+DESCRIPTION", re.IGNORECASE)
_STOP = re.compile(
    r"^\s*(created on|page \d|invoice$|subtotal|total\s|net\s|vat|ust|mwst|"
    r"grand total|amount due|thank you)",
    re.IGNORECASE,
)
#: Column headers leak into the text layer as a row; never an item.
_NOISE = re.compile(r"^\s*(pos\.?|description|amount|unit|total|items)\b", re.IGNORECASE)


def parse_amount(raw: str) -> float:
    """`1`, `1.5`, `1,5`, `1.200,50` -> float. Returns 1.0 on anything unreadable."""
    text = raw.strip()
    if not text:
        return 1.0
    if "," in text and "." in text:
        # Whichever separator comes last is the decimal point.
        text = (
            text.replace(".", "").replace(",", ".")
            if text.rindex(",") > text.rindex(".")
            else text.replace(",", "")
        )
    elif "," in text:
        # A single comma is a decimal comma unless it splits thousands.
        head, _, tail = text.rpartition(",")
        text = f"{head}.{tail}" if len(tail) != 3 or not head else f"{head}{tail}"
    try:
        value = float(text)
    except ValueError:
        return 1.0
    return value if value > 0 else 1.0


def extract_text(pdf_path: str | Path) -> str:
    """Every page's text layer, concatenated. Empty string if unreadable."""
    try:
        from pypdf import PdfReader

        reader = PdfReader(str(pdf_path))
        return "\n".join(page.extract_text() or "" for page in reader.pages)
    except Exception:  # noqa: BLE001 - a broken PDF must not end the round
        log.exception("c2f could not read %s", pdf_path)
        return ""


def parse_line_items(text: str) -> list[LineItem]:
    """Line items in invoice order, keyed by their POS index.

    Only rows after the `POS. DESCRIPTION` header are considered, so addresses
    and invoice numbers cannot be mistaken for items.
    """
    items: list[LineItem] = []
    seen: set[int] = set()
    in_table = False

    for raw_line in text.splitlines():
        line = raw_line.strip()
        if not line:
            continue

        if _HEADER.search(line):
            in_table = True
            continue
        if not in_table:
            continue
        if _STOP.match(line):
            in_table = False
            continue
        if _NOISE.match(line):
            continue

        match = _ROW.match(line)
        if match:
            pos, description, amount, unit = match.groups()
            quantity = parse_amount(amount)
        else:
            match = _BARE_ROW.match(line)
            if not match:
                continue
            pos, description = match.groups()
            quantity, unit = 1.0, ""

        index = int(pos)
        description = description.strip(" .-–—")
        if index in seen or not description:
            continue
        seen.add(index)

        items.append(
            LineItem(
                item_id=str(index),
                index=index,
                description=description,
                quantity=quantity,
                unit=unit.strip() or None,
                raw_text=line,
            )
        )

    items.sort(key=lambda item: item.index)
    return items


def parse_invoice(pdf_path: str | Path) -> list[LineItem]:
    return parse_line_items(extract_text(pdf_path))

"""Load a decrypted case directory into a `CaseBundle`.

Tolerant by design. A missing `policy.txt` costs us accuracy; a raised exception
costs us the round. Every file is optional except the invoice, and even a
zero-item invoice returns a bundle rather than failing.

Policy and description are **not parsed** - they are read verbatim and handed to
the model as-is. Clause extraction would be a lossy pre-filter in front of the
one component able to read the documents properly, and case 0 shows the cost:
its decisive sentence is section 4's "market value at the time of the theft",
which an extractor tuned for exclusions would drop.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import logging
from pathlib import Path

from app.c2f.inference.analyse import CaseBundle
from app.c2f.parsing.invoice import parse_invoice

log = logging.getLogger(__name__)

_IMAGE_SUFFIXES = {".png", ".jpg", ".jpeg", ".webp", ".gif"}
#: Guards against a pathological policy blowing the prompt budget.
MAX_TEXT_CHARS: int = 40_000


def _read_text(path: Path) -> str:
    try:
        return path.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")[:MAX_TEXT_CHARS]
    except OSError:
        log.warning("c2f could not read %s", path)
        return ""


def load_case(case_dir: str | Path, *, case_id: str | None = None) -> CaseBundle:
    """Read one decrypted case folder.

    Files are matched by stem so a `policy.md` or `beschreibung.txt` still lands
    somewhere sensible rather than being silently dropped.
    """
    directory = Path(case_dir)
    policy = ""
    description = ""
    invoice_path: Path | None = None
    images: list[str] = []

    for path in sorted(directory.iterdir()) if directory.is_dir() else []:
        if not path.is_file():
            continue
        stem = path.stem.lower()
        suffix = path.suffix.lower()

        if suffix == ".pdf":
            # Prefer a file that actually says "invoice" when there are several.
            if invoice_path is None or "invoice" in stem:
                invoice_path = path
        elif suffix in _IMAGE_SUFFIXES:
            images.append(str(path))
        elif "polic" in stem or "bedingung" in stem:
            policy = _read_text(path)
        elif "descr" in stem or "damage" in stem or "beschreib" in stem or "schaden" in stem:
            description = _read_text(path)
        elif suffix in {".txt", ".md"} and not description:
            description = _read_text(path)

    items = parse_invoice(invoice_path) if invoice_path else []
    if not items:
        log.error("c2f parsed zero line items from %s", invoice_path or directory)

    return CaseBundle(
        case_id=case_id or directory.name,
        items=items,
        policy=policy,
        description=description,
        image_paths=images,
    )

input.content:
"""The payoff table, executable.

Everything else in the system is an estimate. This module is the ground truth:
given a charge, an acceptance limit, the secret threshold and the cap, it says
exactly what money moves. Used to score a strategy offline against a known `t`,
and later to run the Monte Carlo that picks `b` directly.

Validated against the worked example in `GAME_DESCRIPTION.md` - if that test
fails, this module is wrong, not the test.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from collections.abc import Sequence
from dataclasses import dataclass

#: The insurer's penalty multiplier for rejecting a fair charge: it still owes
#: `a`, plus `0.5a` to the lawyer.
WRONGFUL_REJECT_MULTIPLE: float = 1.5
#: `c >= 4t`. Using the lower bound makes any simulation pessimistic about
#: overcharging, which is the safe direction to be wrong in.
MIN_CAP_MULTIPLE: float = 4.0


@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class Transaction:
    """One issuer-insurer pair on one line item."""

    issuer_receives: float
    insurer_pays: float
    accepted: bool
    fair: bool

    @property
    def label(self) -> str:
        if self.fair and self.accepted:
            return "fair, accepted"
        if self.fair:
            return "wrongful reject"
        if self.accepted:
            return "fraud, accepted"
        return "rightful reject"


def transaction(
    charge: float, limit: float, threshold: float, *, cap: float | None = None
) -> Transaction:
    """Resolve one transaction exactly as the payoff table specifies.

    Note the asymmetry that shapes the whole strategy: in the fair zone the
    issuer is paid whether or not the insurer accepts, so `limit` only changes
    who suffers, never whether the issuer collects.
    """
    fair = charge <= threshold
    accepted = charge <= limit
    ceiling = cap if cap is not None else threshold * MIN_CAP_MULTIPLE

    if accepted:
        paid = charge if fair else min(charge, ceiling)
        return Transaction(paid, paid, accepted=True, fair=fair)
    if fair:
        return Transaction(charge, charge * WRONGFUL_REJECT_MULTIPLE, accepted=False, fair=True)
    return Transaction(0.0, 0.0, accepted=False, fair=False)


@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class ItemScore:
    received: float
    paid: float

    @property
    def net(self) -> float:
        return self.received - self.paid


def score_item(
    our_a: float,
    our_b: float,
    opponents: Sequence[tuple[float, float]],
    threshold: float,
    *,
    cap: float | None = None,
) -> ItemScore:
    """Our net on one line item against a field of `(a, b)` opponents.

    Every team is matched against every other in both roles, so each opponent
    contributes twice: once with us issuing, once with us insuring.
    """
    received = 0.0
    paid = 0.0
    for opponent_a, opponent_b in opponents:
        received += transaction(our_a, opponent_b, threshold, cap=cap).issuer_receives
        paid += transaction(opponent_a, our_b, threshold, cap=cap).insurer_pays
    return ItemScore(received, paid)


def score_field(
    submissions: dict[str, tuple[float, float]],
    threshold: float,
    *,
    cap: float | None = None,
) -> dict[str, ItemScore]:
    """Score every team in a field against each other on one line item.

    Reproduces a whole round, which is what makes the brief's worked example a
    usable regression test.
    """
    out: dict[str, ItemScore] = {}
    for team, (our_a, our_b) in submissions.items():
        others = [pair for name, pair in submissions.items() if name != team]
        out[team] = score_item(our_a, our_b, others, threshold, cap=cap)
    return out

"""Decrypt a case archive.

The archives are AES-256 zips, which `zipfile` cannot read. The starter script
shells out to 7z; we use `pyzipper` instead, for three reasons:

* No external install. 7z is a per-machine dependency that will bite exactly one
  teammate at exactly the wrong moment - it is not present on this machine at
  all, so the 7z path fails here today.
* No subprocess in the 60-second window - process spawn plus disk round-trip,
  gone.
* We can extract straight to memory. Nothing needs to touch the filesystem
  before the model sees it, though we also write it out for the audit trail.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import logging
from pathlib import Path

import pyzipper

log = logging.getLogger(__name__)

#: A case is three or four small files; anything larger is not a case.
MAX_MEMBER_BYTES: int = 32 * 1024 * 1024


class DecryptError(RuntimeError):
    """The archive could not be opened with the given key."""


def archive_path(cases_dir: str | Path, game_id: int) -> Path:
    return Path(cases_dir) / f"case_{game_id:02d}.zip"


def read_members(archive: str | Path, key: str) -> dict[str, bytes]:
    """Every member of the archive, in memory.

    Raises `DecryptError` rather than leaking pyzipper's exception types, so the
    orchestrator has one thing to catch.
    """
    path = Path(archive)
    if not path.exists():
        raise DecryptError(f"missing {path} - stage the archives before the round")

    try:
        with pyzipper.AESZipFile(path) as zip_file:
            zip_file.setpassword(key.encode())
            out: dict[str, bytes] = {}
            for info in zip_file.infolist():
                if info.is_dir():
                    continue
                if info.file_size > MAX_MEMBER_BYTES:
                    log.warning("c2f skipping oversized member %s", info.filename)
                    continue
                # Flatten any directory nesting; case layouts are flat.
                out[Path(info.filename).name] = zip_file.read(info)
    except Exception as error:  # noqa: BLE001 - one failure type for the caller
        raise DecryptError(f"could not decrypt {path.name}: {error}") from error

    if not out:
        raise DecryptError(f"{path.name} decrypted to nothing")
    return out


def extract_case(archive: str | Path, key: str, out_dir: str | Path) -> Path:
    """Decrypt and write the files out. Returns the directory written to.

    We still write to disk even though parsing could work from memory: a round
    that scores oddly is much easier to explain when the exact inputs are
    sitting on disk next to the decision log.
    """
    members = read_members(archive, key)
    directory = Path(out_dir)
    directory.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    for name, data in members.items():
        (directory / name).write_bytes(data)
    return directory

"""Talk to the Claim to Fame API.

Three calls matter: list the games, fetch a game's decryption key, submit prices.
There is deliberately no results endpoint in the handbook, which is why the
learning design cannot use per-matchup outcomes - see `docs/DESIGN.md` section 6.

Two behaviours here exist purely because of the 60-second window:

* The key 403s until `start_time`, so `wait_for_key` polls hard rather than
  sleeping politely. Every 100ms of latency here is 100ms not spent reasoning.
* The client is long-lived and pre-warmed. Establishing TLS inside the window
  costs more than the request itself.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import asyncio
import logging
from collections.abc import Sequence
from dataclasses import dataclass

import httpx

from app.c2f.models import ItemDecision, LineItem
from app.config import get_settings

log = logging.getLogger(__name__)

#: How often to retry the key while the game has not started.
KEY_POLL_INTERVAL: float = 0.2
#: Submissions upsert and last write wins, so a retry is always safe.
SUBMIT_ATTEMPTS: int = 3


class C2FError(RuntimeError):
    """An API call failed in a way the caller has to know about."""


@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class Game:
    id: int
    start_time: str


def build_payload(
    items: Sequence[LineItem],
    decisions: Sequence[ItemDecision],
) -> list[dict[str, float | int]]:
    """The submission body, in invoice order.

    Every parsed line item appears. Omitting one does not opt us out of it - the
    server just applies `charge_price = 0` and `acceptance_limit = 0`, which
    collects nothing and wrongly rejects every fair charge. A missing item is
    the most expensive possible bug, so it cannot happen by omission.
    """
    by_id = {decision.item_id: decision for decision in decisions}
    payload: list[dict[str, float | int]] = []

    for item in items:
        decision = by_id.get(item.item_id)
        index = item.submission_index
        if index <= 0:
            log.error("c2f item %r has no usable submission index; skipping", item.item_id)
            continue
        charge = round(max(decision.a, 0.0), 2) if decision else 0.0
        limit = round(max(decision.b, 0.0), 2) if decision else 0.0
        if decision is None:
            log.error("c2f no decision for item %r; submitting defaults", item.item_id)
        payload.append({"index": index, "charge_price": charge, "acceptance_limit": limit})
    return payload


class C2FClient:
    """One long-lived client per process. Build it before the round starts."""

    def __init__(
        self,
        *,
        api_key: str | None = None,
        base_url: str | None = None,
        timeout: float = 10.0,
        transport: httpx.AsyncBaseTransport | None = None,
    ) -> None:
        settings = get_settings()
        self.api_key = api_key if api_key is not None else settings.team_api_key
        self.base_url = (base_url or settings.c2f_base_url).rstrip("/")
        if not self.api_key:
            raise C2FError("TEAM_API_KEY is not set; cannot reach the Claim to Fame API")

        # `transport` exists so tests can drive the client without a network and
        # without reaching into its internals.
        self._client = httpx.AsyncClient(
            base_url=self.base_url,
            headers={"X-API-Key": self.api_key},
            timeout=timeout,
            transport=transport,
        )

    async def __aenter__(self) -> C2FClient:
        return self

    async def __aexit__(self, *_: object) -> None:
        await self.close()

    async def close(self) -> None:
        await self._client.aclose()

    async def warm(self) -> bool:
        """Open the connection and confirm the key works, before the clock starts."""
        try:
            await self.list_games()
        except C2FError:
            raise
        except Exception as error:  # noqa: BLE001 - warming is best effort
            log.warning("c2f warm-up failed: %s", error)
            return False
        return True

    async def list_games(self) -> list[Game]:
        response = await self._client.get("/api/games/list")
        if response.status_code == 401:
            raise C2FError("401 from /api/games/list - TEAM_API_KEY is missing or invalid")
        if response.status_code != 200:
            raise C2FError(
                f"/api/games/list returned {response.status_code}: {response.text[:200]}"
            )
        return [
            Game(id=int(row["id"]), start_time=str(row.get("start_time", "")))
            for row in response.json()
        ]

    async def get_key(self, game_id: int) -> str | None:
        """The decryption key, or None while the game has not started (403)."""
        response = await self._client.get(f"/api/games/{game_id}/key")
        if response.status_code == 200:
            return str(response.json()["decryption_key"])
        if response.status_code == 403:
            return None
        if response.status_code == 401:
            raise C2FError("401 fetching the decryption key - TEAM_API_KEY is invalid")
        raise C2FError(f"key fetch returned {response.status_code}: {response.text[:200]}")

    async def wait_for_key(self, game_id: int, *, deadline: float = 120.0) -> str:
        """Poll until the key is released. Raises if it never is."""
        loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
        started = loop.time()
        attempts = 0
        while loop.time() - started < deadline:
            attempts += 1
            key = await self.get_key(game_id)
            if key is not None:
                log.info("c2f key for game %s after %d attempt(s)", game_id, attempts)
                return key
            await asyncio.sleep(KEY_POLL_INTERVAL)
        raise C2FError(f"game {game_id} key never released within {deadline:.0f}s")

    async def submit(
        self,
        game_id: int,
        payload: Sequence[dict[str, float | int]],
    ) -> list[dict]:
        """PUT the prices. Upserts, so calling it twice in a round is intended.

        Retried because a lost submission is a zero round, and last write wins
        makes a duplicate harmless.
        """
        last_error: Exception | None = None
        for attempt in range(1, SUBMIT_ATTEMPTS + 1):
            try:
                response = await self._client.put(
                    f"/api/games/{game_id}/submissions", json=list(payload)
                )
            except Exception as error:  # noqa: BLE001 - retry any transport failure
                last_error = error
                log.warning("c2f submit attempt %d failed: %s", attempt, error)
                await asyncio.sleep(0.15 * attempt)
                continue

            if response.status_code == 200:
                log.info("c2f submitted %d line item(s) to game %s", len(payload), game_id)
                return response.json()
            if response.status_code in {401, 403, 404, 422}:
                # None of these get better by retrying.
                raise C2FError(
                    f"submit rejected with {response.status_code}: {response.text[:300]}"
                )
            last_error = C2FError(f"submit returned {response.status_code}")
            await asyncio.sleep(0.15 * attempt)

        raise C2FError(f"submit failed after {SUBMIT_ATTEMPTS} attempts: {last_error}")

"""Run one round end to end.

    uv run python -m app.c2f.run --game 0            # analyse, print, do NOT submit
    uv run python -m app.c2f.run --game 0 --submit   # actually send the prices

Dry run is the default on purpose: submitting is outward-facing under our team
identity, and last-write-wins means a careless run can overwrite a good one.

NOTE: the repo also has a top-level `c2f/` package with its own runner
(`make <game_id>`). Two live submit paths for one team is a hazard - pick one
before a real round. See `docs/DESIGN.md` section 14.

This is the sequential version, for testing outside a live round. The live
orchestrator adds the safety-net submission at T+8 and the hard deadline at
T+55; see `docs/DESIGN.md` section 2.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import asyncio
import logging
import time
from pathlib import Path

from app.c2f.api_client import C2FClient, C2FError, build_payload
from app.c2f.decision.guardrails import blocking, check, repair
from app.c2f.decision.optimizer import decide
from app.c2f.decrypt import DecryptError, archive_path, extract_case
from app.c2f.inference.analyse import analyse_case, heuristic_inferences
from app.c2f.models import Calibration, ItemDecision
from app.c2f.parsing.case import load_case
from app.config import get_settings

log = logging.getLogger("c2f.run")

REPO_ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[3]
CASES_DIR = REPO_ROOT / "cases"


def decrypt_case(game_id: int, key: str) -> Path:
    """Extract `cases/case_NN.zip` next to the archive. Pure Python, no 7z."""
    try:
        return extract_case(
            archive_path(CASES_DIR, game_id), key, CASES_DIR / f"case_{game_id:02d}"
        )
    except DecryptError as error:
        raise C2FError(str(error)) from error


async def run_round(game_id: int, *, submit: bool, use_llm: bool) -> list[ItemDecision]:
    settings = get_settings()
    started = time.monotonic()

    def mark(label: str) -> None:
        print(f"  [{time.monotonic() - started:5.1f}s] {label}")

    print(f"\n=== game {game_id} ===")
    async with C2FClient() as client:
        await client.warm()
        mark("client warm, key accepted")

        games = await client.list_games()
        print(f"  {len(games)} game(s) available")
        if not any(g.id == game_id for g in games):
            print(f"  ! game {game_id} is not in the list; continuing anyway")

        key = await client.wait_for_key(game_id)
        mark(f"decryption key: {key}")

        case_dir = decrypt_case(game_id, key)
        mark(f"decrypted -> {case_dir}")

        bundle = load_case(case_dir, case_id=str(game_id))
        mark(f"parsed {len(bundle.items)} line item(s)")
        for item in bundle.items:
            unit = item.unit or ""
            print(f"      {item.index:>3}  qty={item.quantity:g} {unit:<6} {item.description}")

        if use_llm and settings.anthropic_api_key:
            result = await analyse_case(bundle)
            mark(f"inference done: {result.calls_ok}")
            inferences = result.inferences
        else:
            reason = "--no-llm" if not use_llm else "ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is empty"
            print(f"  ! semantic layer skipped ({reason}); using the heuristic fallback")
            inferences = heuristic_inferences(bundle.items)

        decisions = [
            decide(item, inference, calibration=Calibration())
            for item, inference in zip(bundle.items, inferences, strict=True)
        ]
        violations = check(bundle.items, decisions, inferences=inferences)
        if blocking(violations):
            print("  ! blocking violations, repairing:")
            for violation in blocking(violations):
                print(f"      {violation}")
            decisions = repair(decisions)
            violations = check(bundle.items, decisions, inferences=inferences)
        for violation in violations:
            print(f"      warning: {violation}")
        mark("guardrails passed" if not blocking(violations) else "guardrails STILL failing")

        payload = build_payload(bundle.items, decisions)
        print(f"\n  {'idx':>4}{'charge a':>12}{'limit b':>12}{'p_valid':>10}{'sigma':>8}  item")
        for row, item, decision in zip(payload, bundle.items, decisions, strict=False):
            print(
                f"  {row['index']:>4}{row['charge_price']:>12.2f}{row['acceptance_limit']:>12.2f}"
                f"{decision.p_valid:>10.2f}{decision.sigma_log:>8.3f}  {item.description}"
            )

        if submit:
            confirmation = await client.submit(game_id, payload)
            mark(f"SUBMITTED {len(confirmation)} line item(s)")
        else:
            mark("dry run - nothing submitted (pass --submit to send)")

    return decisions


def main() -> None:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Run one Claim to Fame round.")
    parser.add_argument("--game", type=int, default=0, help="game id (0 is the test game)")
    parser.add_argument("--submit", action="store_true", help="actually send the prices")
    parser.add_argument("--no-llm", action="store_true", help="skip inference, use the fallback")
    parser.add_argument("-v", "--verbose", action="store_true")
    args = parser.parse_args()

    logging.basicConfig(
        level=logging.INFO if args.verbose else logging.WARNING,
        format="%(levelname)s %(name)s: %(message)s",
    )

    try:
        asyncio.run(run_round(args.game, submit=args.submit, use_llm=not args.no_llm))
    except C2FError as error:
        raise SystemExit(f"\n  x {error}") from error


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""The payoff table. Anchored on the worked example in the brief."""

from __future__ import annotations

import pytest

from app.c2f.decision.payoff import score_field, score_item, transaction


def test_the_briefs_worked_example_reproduces_exactly():
    """Three teams, one windshield, t=100. The brief states the answer, so we check it.

    If this fails, the payoff module is wrong - not the numbers below.
    """
    field = {
        "Alpha Squad": (100.0, 130.0),
        "Beta Dynamics": (150.0, 90.0),
        "Delta Strategies": (100.0, 110.0),
    }
    scores = score_field(field, threshold=100.0)

    assert scores["Alpha Squad"].received == 200.0
    assert scores["Alpha Squad"].paid == 100.0
    assert scores["Alpha Squad"].net == 100.0

    assert scores["Delta Strategies"].received == 200.0
    assert scores["Delta Strategies"].paid == 100.0
    assert scores["Delta Strategies"].net == 100.0

    assert scores["Beta Dynamics"].received == 0.0
    assert scores["Beta Dynamics"].paid == 300.0
    assert scores["Beta Dynamics"].net == -300.0


def test_the_field_is_zero_sum_apart_from_lawyer_penalties():
    field = {"a": (100.0, 130.0), "b": (150.0, 90.0), "c": (100.0, 110.0)}
    scores = score_field(field, threshold=100.0)
    # Two wrongful rejects at 100 each burn 0.5 * 100 twice.
    assert sum(s.net for s in scores.values()) == pytest.approx(-100.0)


# ---------- the four cells of the table ----------


def test_fair_and_accepted_pays_the_charge():
    result = transaction(80.0, limit=100.0, threshold=100.0)
    assert (result.issuer_receives, result.insurer_pays) == (80.0, 80.0)
    assert result.label == "fair, accepted"


def test_fair_and_rejected_still_pays_the_issuer_plus_the_lawyer():
    """The result the whole strategy hangs on: rejection does not save the money."""
    result = transaction(80.0, limit=50.0, threshold=100.0)
    assert result.issuer_receives == 80.0
    assert result.insurer_pays == 120.0
    assert result.label == "wrongful reject"


def test_fraud_and_accepted_pays_up_to_the_cap():
    result = transaction(500.0, limit=600.0, threshold=100.0, cap=400.0)
    assert result.issuer_receives == 400.0
    assert result.insurer_pays == 400.0
    assert result.label == "fraud, accepted"


def test_fraud_and_rejected_moves_nothing():
    result = transaction(500.0, limit=100.0, threshold=100.0)
    assert (result.issuer_receives, result.insurer_pays) == (0.0, 0.0)
    assert result.label == "rightful reject"


def test_the_boundaries_are_inclusive():
    """`a <= t` is fair and `a <= b` is accepted, both inclusive."""
    assert transaction(100.0, limit=100.0, threshold=100.0).fair
    assert transaction(100.0, limit=100.0, threshold=100.0).accepted


def test_the_default_cap_is_four_times_the_threshold():
    assert transaction(1_000.0, limit=2_000.0, threshold=100.0).issuer_receives == 400.0


def test_an_uncovered_item_makes_every_positive_charge_fraud():
    assert not transaction(0.01, limit=100.0, threshold=0.0).fair

"""Prompts for the semantic layer.

Design rules these encode:

* One call sees the **whole invoice** and returns an array. Per-item calls do not
  fit in 60 seconds, and an item-at-a-time view cannot spot a duplicated line or
  a labour charge inconsistent with the parts.
* `p_valid` is asked for **jointly**. `p_covered * p_related` understates it
  because the two are strongly dependent.
* Prices are asked for **per unit**. The quantity multiply happens in code.
* The pricing call **gets the policy**. An early version withheld it on the
  reasoning that a policy says nothing about market rates. Case 0 disproves
  that: its section 4 pays market value at the time of theft, so a line reading
  "New Bike" is worth EUR 420, not the price of a new bicycle. The basis of
  indemnity *is* the price, and it outweighs any market estimate.
* A **stated** value must collapse the spread. On case 0 a plausible-looking
  +-6% range costs EUR 396 against an oracle, EUR 210 of it from `b` landing
  six euros under `t`. Hedging a figure the documents give you is the expensive
  choice, not the cautious one.
* No prompt is told about `a`, `b`, the 2/3 rule, or the payoff table. The
  semantic layer answers "what do the documents imply"; the decision is not its
  business, and telling it about the incentives only invites it to skew the
  estimate.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from collections.abc import Sequence

from app.c2f.models import LineItem

VALIDITY_SYSTEM = """\
You are a senior insurance claims examiner. You are given an insurance policy, a \
damage report, and the line items of a repair invoice.

For each line item, estimate the probability that it is BOTH covered by the policy \
AND reasonably necessary as a consequence of the reported damage. Estimate that \
joint probability directly - do not estimate two separate probabilities and \
multiply them.

Calibration matters more than caution. If an item is plainly part of the described \
repair and plainly inside the policy, say 0.97, not 0.8. If the policy explicitly \
excludes it, say 0.02. Reserve middling values for genuine ambiguity.

Return ONLY a JSON array, one object per line item, no prose:
[
  {
    "item_id": "<exactly the id given to you>",
    "p_valid": 0.0,
    "p_covered": 0.0,
    "p_related": 0.0,
    "evidence": "<one sentence, quoting the policy clause or damage detail>",
    "exclusion_hit": "<policy exclusion that applies, or empty>"
  }
]
"""

PRICING_SYSTEM = """\
You are a senior insurance claims assessor deciding what a line item is WORTH \
under a specific policy. You are not quoting a shop price - you are setting the \
amount the insurer owes.

Work in this order:

1. Find the policy's BASIS OF INDEMNITY - the clause saying what it pays. It is \
usually one of: market value at the time of loss, replacement cost (new for old), \
repair cost, or depreciated value. Apply THAT basis, not the wording of the \
invoice line. An invoice line reading "New Bike", under a policy that reimburses \
the market value at the time of the theft, is worth that market value - not the \
price of a new bicycle.
2. If the documents STATE the relevant amount (a stated value, an appraisal, a \
sum insured, a purchase price with a date), that figure is the answer. Anchor on \
it and make the spread NEARLY ZERO - put all five quantiles within a couple of \
percent of each other. Do not widen the range to hedge; a stated value is the \
strongest evidence you will get.
3. Otherwise estimate from the market, and let the spread reflect your genuine \
uncertainty: narrow for a commodity part you know well, wide for a vague \
description.
4. Apply any sum insured or deductible the policy states.

Rules:
- Price ONE UNIT of the item, not the whole line. Ignore the quantity entirely.
- For labour lines, one unit is one hour (or whatever unit is stated).
- Include applicable VAT in the figures. Prices are in EUR.
- q10 is a defensibly low figure, q50 your best single estimate, q90 a \
defensibly high one.

Return ONLY a JSON array, one object per line item, no prose:
[
  {
    "item_id": "<exactly the id given to you>",
    "q10": 0, "q25": 0, "q50": 0, "q75": 0, "q90": 0,
    "indemnity_basis": "<the clause you applied>",
    "unit_basis": "<what one unit is>",
    "price_basis": "<one sentence on where the number comes from>",
    "confidence": "high|medium|low"
  }
]
"""

SKEPTIC_SYSTEM = """\
You are an adversarial claims auditor. Assume the invoice may be padded and look \
for it: work that is not needed for the described damage, quantities that exceed \
what the job requires, replacement where repair would do, premium parts on a \
standard repair, duplicated lines, labour hours inconsistent with the parts fitted.

You are looking across the WHOLE invoice, so use cross-item evidence.

For each line item return a multiplier on the fair unit price - 1.0 if you find \
nothing wrong, down to 0.5 if the line looks substantially padded. Do not exceed \
1.0; you argue prices down, never up.

Return ONLY a JSON array, one object per line item, no prose:
[
  {
    "item_id": "<exactly the id given to you>",
    "suggested_multiplier": 1.0,
    "inflation_flags": ["..."],
    "qty_plausible": true
  }
]
"""


def render_items(items: Sequence[LineItem]) -> str:
    """The invoice as the models see it. Ids are ours, and they must come back."""
    lines = []
    for item in items:
        unit = f" {item.unit}" if item.unit else ""
        lines.append(
            f"- item_id={item.item_id} | quantity={item.quantity:g}{unit} | {item.description}"
        )
    return "\n".join(lines)


def case_context(
    items: Sequence[LineItem],
    *,
    policy: str = "",
    description: str = "",
    include_policy: bool = True,
) -> str:
    """One user message carrying the whole case.

    `include_policy` exists to drop the policy block, but nothing does that now:
    the pricing call needs it too, because the basis-of-indemnity clause sets the
    price. See the module docstring.
    """
    blocks: list[str] = []
    if include_policy and policy.strip():
        blocks.append(f"=== INSURANCE POLICY ===\n{policy.strip()}")
    if description.strip():
        blocks.append(f"=== DAMAGE DESCRIPTION ===\n{description.strip()}")
    blocks.append(f"=== INVOICE LINE ITEMS ({len(items)}) ===\n{render_items(items)}")
    blocks.append(f"Return exactly {len(items)} objects, one per item_id above, in the same order.")
    return "\n\n".join(blocks)

---

## 12. What case 0 taught us

Case 0 is a single line item, `New Bike`, quantity 1. The whole case turns on
policy section 4: the insurer reimburses **the market value at the time of the
theft**, and the description states that value as EUR 420. Cover conditions are
met (locked to a lamp post) and no exclusion applies. So `t = 420`, and an
invoice line reading "New Bike" is worth EUR 420 rather than a new bicycle's
price. QuantCo's own starter script hints at it: its placeholder values are
`charge_price = 410`, `acceptance_limit = 430`.

Scored offline against a field of five plausible opponents (`decision/payoff.py`,
which reproduces the brief's worked example exactly):

| strategy | a | b | net |
|---|---|---|---|
| oracle (knows `t`) | 420.00 | 420.00 | **+1280** |
| ours, confident belief | 418.65 | 420.53 | **+1273** |
| the `c2f/` engine's mock belief (380/420/450) | 402.50 | 410.55 | +983 |
| ours, tight belief (+-6%) | 382.83 | 413.99 | +884 |
| ours, heuristic fallback | 356.46 | 45.35 | +552 |
| ours, loose belief (+-25%) | 330.02 | 389.66 | +420 |
| ours, missed the clause | 659.33 | 692.63 | -161 |
| naive, prices a new bike | 800.00 | 900.00 | -820 |

Three conclusions, all of which changed the code:

**The decision layer is not the bottleneck.** Given a correct belief it lands
within 0.5% of an oracle that knows `t`. Every remaining euro is in the semantic
layer. Effort goes there.

**The pricing call needs the policy.** An earlier version withheld it, reasoning
that a policy says nothing about market rates. That reasoning is wrong: the
basis-of-indemnity clause *is* the price, and it outweighs any market estimate.
Withholding it is the difference between +1273 and -161 on this case. The pricing
prompt now leads with "find the basis of indemnity and apply THAT basis, not the
wording of the invoice line".

**A stated value must collapse the spread.** The `tight (+-6%)` row loses EUR 396
against the oracle, and EUR 210 of that is one error: `b = 413.99` sits EUR 6
below `t`, so it wrongfully rejects a fair EUR 420 charge and pays the 1.5x
penalty. When the documents state the amount, hedging the range is not caution -
it is the expensive choice. The prompt now asks for a near-zero spread in that
case, and the `confident` row is what that produces. This applies to any
implementation using a 1/3-quantile rule, including the `c2f/` engine: its
triangular belief puts `b` below its own mid by construction, so a spread wider
than reality is what costs it the 210.

## 13. Confirmed API constraints

- Line items are addressed by `index`, the invoice POS column. Never renumber.
- **There is no results endpoint.** List games, fetch key, submit - that is all.
  Per-matchup outcomes are not exposed, so Branch A of section 6 is unavailable
  and the two global knobs are the learning mechanism. The leaderboard is the
  only feedback channel.
- Omitted line items default to `0 / 0` and still participate, so every parsed
  item must appear in the payload. `b = 0` on a covered item pays the penalty to
  every opponent.
- 101 games exist (0-100). Game 0 is a permanent test game.
- Archives are AES-256 zips. We read them with `pyzipper` rather than shelling
  out to 7z: no per-machine install, no subprocess in the 60-second window. 7z is
  not installed on at least one team machine, so the subprocess path fails there.

## 14. Two engines currently live in this repo

| | `backend/app/c2f/` (this design) | `c2f/` (the other engine) |
|---|---|---|
| LLM calls | 3 concurrent, structured | 1 call, fast+full passes |
| belief | 5-knot ladder, log-space, lognormal tails | triangular `t_low/t_mid/t_high` |
| `a` | `argmax a*S(a)` | `t_mid * (1 - 0.25 * spread)`, floored at `t_low` |
| `b` | `Q(1 - (2/3)/p_valid)`, exact | `tri_quantile(.., 1/3)` |
| decrypt | `pyzipper`, in-process | subprocess |
| entry point | `python -m app.c2f.run` | `make <game_id>` |
| offline scorer | `decision/payoff.py` | none |

They agree on the economics that matter - the 2/3 rule, `b = 0` when uncovered,
still charging on an uncovered item - which is a good sign for both.

Two differences are substantive rather than cosmetic:

* `a = t_mid * (1 - K * spread)` can never exceed `t_mid`. That forgoes R2: when
  our belief is genuinely wide the revenue-maximising charge sits *above* the
  median, and it forgoes the fraud-zone term entirely.
* Only this design has an offline scorer, so only this one can answer "would that
  change have made us money on the cases we have already seen".

**Pick one before a live round.** Two submit paths for one team, with
last-write-wins semantics and a 60-second window, is a way to lose a round to a
race between our own processes.
MDEOF

Two things I fixed along the way rather than just re-adding:

**`cases/` had been deleted too** — all 101 archives, gone and untracked so unrecoverable by `git checkout`. They were in commit `fe24f2c`; I restored them to the working tree and unstaged them so they stay gitignored. Worth knowing that commit is your only copy.

**My heredoc mangled the pricing prompt** into 400-char joined lines when I first re-applied it. Content was right, source was unlintable. Rewritten with proper continuations and verified the string renders as 26 lines / 1,884 chars containing `BASIS OF INDEMNITY`.

## The thing you should actually decide

The revert brought in a **second complete engine** at `c2f/` — extract, price, submit, run, Makefile, its own tests. It independently derives the same ⅔ rule and the same "still charge on uncovered items" result, which is a good sign for both designs. But there are now **two submit paths for one team**, with last-write-wins and a 60-second window. That's a way to lose a round to a race between our own processes. Comparison table is in `DESIGN.md` §14.

Two differences that aren't cosmetic:

- Its `a = t_mid × (1 − 0.25 × spread)` can never exceed `t_mid`. That gives up R2 — when the belief is genuinely wide, the revenue-maximising charge sits *above* the median — and gives up the fraud-zone term entirely.
- Only this side has an offline scorer, so only this side can answer "would that change have made money on cases we've already seen".

Its prompt does *not* have the bug mine had — it explicitly checks "amount of indemnity". But it never says *collapse the spread when a value is stated*, and that's the €210 on case 0. Its `runs/game_00.json` was `"provider": "mock"` with hardcoded `380/420/450`, scoring **983** against the oracle's 1280. That one line in its prompt is worth adding regardless of which engine you keep.

`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is still empty, so neither engine has called a real model yet. That remains the biggest unverified assumption in either design.

content.text:
Game 2 opened 13:12:37 and was already `completed` by 13:15:42. The window is ~1 minute as the brief states. Our game-1 run at 13:06 was never going to land.

## Why we lost game 1

**Two independent failures. Either one alone loses the round.**

**1. The run started 6m09s late.** Game 1 opened 13:00:00Z; `started_at` in your log is 13:06:09Z. The fast answer was ready at +394s and the full at +404s, against a ~60s window. Even with submitting enabled, both would have been rejected as late.

**2. `--no-submit` was passed.** Both entries record `"skipped (--no-submit)"`. This wasn't a tooling default — `make 1` submits, and the flag is opt-in at `c2f/run.py:86`. It was explicit on that invocation.

So the server applied defaults `a=0, b=0`.

## Where the −8,273.70 came from

| side | what happened | result |
|---|---|---|
| issuer | `a=0` on all 18 items × 16 opponents | 288 transactions "accepted", income **€0** |
| insurer | `b=0` rejected all 45 non-zero incoming charges | 27 were **fair** → paid 1.5a each |

Σ of those 27 charges = 5,515.80; × 1.5 = **8,273.70** exactly. The other 18 were genuinely fraudulent and correctly rejected at zero cost. The remaining 243 opponents also charged 0.

Thirteen of seventeen teams share that exact score — it is the "submitted nothing" signature, not a strategy failure.

## What the values you computed were actually worth

Scored against provable ground truth only (charges the engine confirmed as fair, so `t ≥ a`):

| | insurer cost | guaranteed income | net |
|---|---|---|---|
| actual (defaults) | 8,273.70 | 0 | **−8,273.70** |
| your `full` / gpt-5 | 6,806.74 | 27,552 | **≥ +20,745** |
| your `fast` / gpt-5-mini | 6,215.15 | 11,420 | **≥ +5,205** |

Those income figures are *lower bounds* — they count only 7 of 18 items, the ones where our `a` sits below a proven `t`. Fair charges are paid by every opponent regardless of their limit, so that money was certain.

The miss cost roughly **29,000**, against a first place of 33,436. The pipeline was good enough to win game 1.

## Two genuine model errors, worth fixing

**Item 18** — "premium hardwood skirting boards (upgrade from pre-loss softwood)". Both models set `t=0` because it's an upgrade. Proven `t ≥ 98.02`. The *upgrade* isn't covered, but the like-for-like softwood replacement is: an upgrade line is worth **the pre-loss-standard equivalent, not zero**. Same applies to item 4 (stone-for-ceramic, charged 1728 with `b=0`). That's a systematic, generalisable prompt fix.

**Item 1** — "clean / dry conservatory rug". gpt-5 ruled it not covered (loose furnishing, 4.2.3) and set `b=0`; proven `t ≥ 122.94`. gpt-5-mini had it covered at `t_mid=120` and was right. Note this one is *confident and wrong*, so a continuous `p_valid` wouldn't have saved it — 0.5 is still below the ⅔ bar. Model disagreement is the signal here, not uncertainty within one model.

Broader exposure: `full` set `b=0` on 8 of 18 items. Each wrong `b=0` pays 1.5a to all 16 opponents.

## Correction to something I told you earlier

I said there's no results endpoint and per-item threshold learning was impossible. **That was wrong.** The leaderboard has undocumented endpoints — `/leaderboard/api/{performance,matrix,matchup,transactions,games}` — and `transactions` gives per-matchup outcomes. Game 1 alone yields 27 exact lower bounds on `t`. The Branch A learning design is available after all, and `docs/DESIGN.md` §13 needs correcting.

## The fix that actually matters

Not "remember the flag". 100 games, one every ~12.6 minutes, each with a ~60-second window. The Makefile comment says *"start it a few seconds before the game opens"* — a manual protocol that will miss rounds. This needs a scheduler that polls `/api/games`, wakes before each `start_time`, runs, and submits — plus the T+8 safety-net submission so a slow model still produces something.

Game 3 opens at **13:25:15Z**. Not submitting anything, per your instruction — tell me when you want that scheduler built.

Now it's clear. Answer to your question, in order of what actually matters:

## Is the mathematical model wired?

Wired and verified end to end, but it had **never once run on real model output** until just now — and doing so exposed a bug that had been silently corrupting it.

`extract_json` scanned for `{` before `[`, so on a JSON *array* it returned only the first object. On the 18-item case that meant **item 1 got real inference and items 2–18 all fell back to the heuristic** — with no error logged. That's why my case-1 run showed 15 identical rows. Fixed, with a regression test that asserts on the *last* array element rather than the first. 126 tests pass.

Also: `LLM_PROVIDER=anthropic` with an empty key, so every call failed and degraded. Your OpenAI key works — I ran through it with `LLM_PROVIDER=openai LLM_MODEL=gpt-5-mini`. That needs to become the default in `.env` or the pipeline is dead weight.

## Your model vs mine: same LLM, two maths

I fed both pricing functions the **identical** gpt-5-mini beliefs from your game-1 log. The `b` values come out nearly the same (112.05 vs 112.54, 168.08 vs 168.99) — both implement the same ⅓-quantile rule, so `b` is not a differentiator at all. The only difference is `a`, and mine is higher on every line.

Scored against where `t` actually sits:

| strategy | t = proven bound | t ≥ t_mid |
|---|---|---|
| yours, K=0.5 (current) | **12,785** | 38,625 |
| yours, K=0.25 (before) | 5,205 | **48,505** |
| mine, μ=1.0 | 4,989 | **47,818** |
| mine, μ=0.85 | 3,113 | 39,518 |

**The decision math is not where the money is.** Your K=0.25 and my optimiser land within 1.5% of each other. Once the shading matches, the two formulas are equivalent in practice. My design's edge isn't a better formula — it's that `mu_shift` is a *fitted* parameter rather than a hand-tuned constant, and we finally have data to fit it.

## The finding you should act on

You raised `K_UNCERTAINTY` from 0.25 to 0.5 because game 2 looked like ~15% over-pricing. **Game 1's data says the opposite.** Of 8 items where `t` is measurable, 5 have `t` *strictly above* `t_mid`:

| item | t_mid | proven t ≥ | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| 9 | 260 | 409.79 | ≥1.58 |
| 7 | 130 | 182.13 | ≥1.40 |
| 2, 13 | 180 | 227.66 | ≥1.26 |
| 1 | 120 | 122.94 | ≥1.02 |

Zero items show evidence of over-estimation — the other three just have weak bounds. Median lower bound on `t/t_mid` is 1.14. In that regime, K=0.5 costs about **10,000 per round** versus K=0.25.

Caveat worth stating: these bounds come from other teams' charges that were ruled fair, so they're valid lower bounds but a biased-low estimate of `t`. The direction of the bias only strengthens the conclusion — real `t` is at least this high.

Game 2 has completed, so the same analysis is available for it. That's the honest way to settle K: fit it on both rounds rather than reacting to one.

## Ranked by euros

1. **Submit at all** — ~29,000/round. Two independent failures in game 1 (6 minutes late, `--no-submit`).
2. **Stop over-shading `a`** — ~10,000/round. Revert K to 0.25, or fit `mu_shift` from transaction data.
3. **Upgrade lines aren't worth zero** — item 18 proved `t ≥ 98` where both models said 0. An upgrade is worth the pre-loss-standard equivalent.
4. The pricing formula itself — worth ~1.5%. Not the priority.

Now I can answer that precisely, and the answer is encouraging.

## error404's lead is a one-off, not a trend

| | game 1 | game 2 | game 3 | total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| error404 ai | **33,436** | 4,803 | 403 | 38,642 |
| AsianSuperNerds | −8,274 | **11,651** | 0 | 3,377 |

**87% of their total is game 1** — the round where 13 of 17 teams submitted nothing and their fair charges collected `a` from everyone plus the 1.5× penalty. That cannot repeat now the field is awake.

Since everyone woke up: **games 2+3, we scored 11,651 to their 5,206.** We were #1 in game 2, ahead of Codacabana's 10,355. The 35,265 gap closes at roughly 3,200/game at that differential, so ~11 rounds, with ~97 left.

## What won us game 2

Income 14,215, insurer cost 2,564 → net 11,651. Two correct fair charges produced 97% of it:

| item | our charge | outcome |
|---|---|---|
| 4 | 555.00 | fair → paid by all 16 = 8,880 |
| 1 | 310.00 | fair → paid by all 16 = 4,960 |
| 2,3,5,6,7 | 12–60 | fraud → 2–3 lenient reviewers each = 375 |

error404 only priced item 4 and charged **525.35** where we charged **555** — both fair, so `t ≥ 555`. Their shading cost them 475 on that one item. That's direct empirical confirmation of the `K=0.5` finding: on the one item where we can measure it, charging *less* lost money.

## Your insurer side is already solved

Cumulative: **0 wrongfully accepted, and all 27 wrongful rejections were game 1's `b=0`.** Games 2 and 3 had zero of each — perfect classification. Insurer cost fell from 8,274 to 2,564. Don't touch `b`; it's doing exactly what the ⅔ rule promises. Every remaining euro is on `a`.

## The one thing game 3 exposes

Game 3 was two items, `t` very low on both. We charged above every opponent's limit and earned **0**. error404 charged ~101 and ~100, got rejected by 14, and **2 lenient reviewers paid each → 403 at zero risk.**

We know our low free-shots work — in game 2 our 12–60 charges caught 2–3 acceptors apiece. So game 3 wasn't a strategy failure, it was a *level* failure: `a = 0.6 × t_if_covered` scales with the item's hypothetical value, which on an expensive-but-worthless item lands far above anyone's limit.

The fix is to aim the free shot at the lenient tail rather than at a fraction of the item's value. Two of sixteen teams accept around €100, so on a believed-worthless item the charge should sit near that, regardless of what the item would have cost if covered. That's the `argmax a·G(a)` term — and we now have three rounds of transaction data to fit `G` from.

Priorities unchanged in rank, updated in size: never miss a round; stop over-shading fair charges (`K` back to 0.25); cap the free-shot at the observed lenient-acceptance level rather than scaling it with item value.
Should we lower our a when t is low?

Careful — that question conflates two different situations, and the answers point in opposite directions.

**When we *believe* `t` is low**, `a` already scales down automatically: `argmax a·S(a)` is proportional to our median. Nothing to change.

**When we believe the item is worthless** (`t ≈ 0`), `S(a) ≈ 0` for every positive `a`, so the objective collapses to `a·G(a)` — pure opponent acceptance. The item's hypothetical value drops out of the maths entirely, which is exactly why `a = 0.6 × t_if_covered` is the wrong rule. But whether that means *lower* depends on the shape of `G`. Now I can answer properly, with error bars.

## No — and in fact the opposite, but stop scaling it with the item's value

Two separate mistakes, in opposite directions:

**Game 2: our free shots were too LOW.** We charged €12–60 on the five worthless items and collected €375. At those levels `a·G(a)` is 2.83–6.57 per opponent; at €100–200 it's **14.00**. Same zero risk, roughly triple the return.

**Game 3: our free shots were too HIGH.** Nobody accepted, so we collected nothing — our charges sat above even the most lenient reviewer's limit.

Both follow from the same root cause: `a = 0.6 × t_if_covered` ties the charge to the item's hypothetical value, which is the one quantity that provably does **not** affect the answer. When `S(a) ≈ 0`, revenue is `a·G(a)`, and `G` is a property of *opponents*, not of the item.

## Where the honest uncertainty is

Censoring rate is 24.5% — a charge nobody accepted leaves no record of its size, and big charges are the likeliest to be refused by everyone. So the curve is optimistic exactly where the sample is thinnest:

| band | observations | `a·G(a)` |
|---|---|---|
| 0–25 | 3 | 2.83 |
| 25–50 | 9 | 5.00 |
| 50–100 | 6 | 6.57 |
| **100–200** | **12** | **14.00** |
| 200–400 | 1 | 17.11 |
| 400+ | 2 | 46.27 optimistic / **12.62** worst-case |

Under the worst case — every censored charge sitting in the top band — 400+ drops *below* the 100–200 band. So the evidence supports charging up to about **€100–200 flat** and does not support going beyond it. That is precisely where error404 sat in game 3 (€100.40 and €101.32), collecting 403 at zero risk while we collected nothing.

## Concrete rule

On an item believed worthless: `b = 0` (unchanged), and `a` ≈ €120–150 **flat**, regardless of `t_if_covered`. Revisit the band as censoring resolves — every round adds observations, and `argmax a·G(a)` should eventually be fit rather than hand-set.

## Keep it in proportion

Fixing this is worth roughly **+750/round** (five worthless items × ~224 each, versus the 375 we actually got). Compare: game 2's two correct fair charges produced **13,840**. So this is a real free improvement, but it's second-order — do it after never missing a round and after reverting `K` to 0.25.

One forward risk worth noting: the transaction feed names issuers, so opponents can profile us. A team that always charges €150 on junk lines is easy to filter out, and `G` will shrink as the field learns. That argues for fitting `G` continuously rather than fixing a constant now.

Both modules already exist and do real work — `truth.py` recovers `t` intervals from the matchup equations (both bounds, stronger than the lower bounds I was computing by hand), and `feedback.py` extracts every team's charges plus implied `b` bounds. So the learning *inputs* exist; nothing feeds them back into pricing yet.

Here is the model as it actually stands.

## 1. Estimating `t` — a distribution, never a point

**Stage 1, LLM votes.** Three gpt-5 calls in parallel, each seeing policy + description + invoice verbatim. Per line item each returns `covered`, `related`, the clause cited, and a triple `(t_low, t_mid, t_high)` — its belief about the gross total a frugal claims expert would still accept. If not covered: all zero plus `t_if_covered`.

**Stage 2, aggregation** (`ensemble.py`): `covered` by majority, a tie counting as *not* covered. `t_low/t_mid/t_high` = median over the votes that said covered. That median is the only place model disagreement gets absorbed.

**Stage 3, representation.** The triple becomes a **triangular density on `[t_low, t_high]` with mode `t_mid`**. That is the belief about `t`, and everything downstream reads only from it.

The CDF is closed-form, which is why the triangle was chosen:

```
F(x) = (x−lo)² / ((hi−lo)(mode−lo))            x ≤ mode
     = 1 − (hi−x)² / ((hi−lo)(hi−mode))        x > mode
```

## 2. `b` — derived from the payoff table, not tuned

Facing a charge `a`, with `p = P(t ≥ a)`:

- accept → pay `a`
- reject → pay `1.5a` with probability `p` (it was fair), `0` otherwise

So `E[reject] = 1.5a·p`, and accepting is better exactly when

```
a ≤ 1.5·a·p    ⟺    p ≥ 2/3
```

Therefore `b = sup{a : P(t ≥ a) ≥ 2/3}`, i.e. the value where `F(b) = 1/3` — the **⅓-quantile of the belief**:

```python
b = tri_quantile(t_low, t_mid, t_high, 1/3)
  = lo + sqrt((1/3)·(hi−lo)·(mid−lo))          # when that lands below the mode
```

Not covered → `b = 0`, because then `P(t ≥ a) = 0 < 2/3` for every positive `a`.

The ⅓ is **not a tunable constant** — it falls out of the 1.5 penalty. Both engines derive it independently and agree. Empirically it's been flawless: 0 wrongfully accepted and 0 wrongfully rejected across games 2 and 3.

## 3. `a` — this is the heuristic half

**Live formula** (`price.py`):

```python
spread = (t_high − t_low) / t_mid
a = max(t_low, t_mid · (1 − K·spread))      K = 0.5
a = 0.6 · t_if_covered                       # when not covered
```

That is a hand-tuned downward shade off the mode. It is *not* derived from the payoff table, and `K` and `0.6` are free parameters set by eye.

**My engine's formula** (`decision/optimizer.py`) derives it instead. From the payoff table's left column, a fair charge is paid whether or not the insurer accepts — so the opponent's limit only matters above `t`:

```
R(a) = a·S(a)  +  min(a,c)·(1 − S(a))·G(a)        S(a) = P(t ≥ a)
       └ fair: paid by everyone ┘   └ fraud: only lenient reviewers ┘

a* = argmax R(a)      over 2000 log-spaced points in [0.02·q50, 4·q50]
```

With no opponent model this is `argmax a·S(a)`, which for a lognormal belief solves `hazard(z) = σ` — landing near the 24th percentile at `σ=0.4` and near the 72nd at `σ=1.2`. Uncertainty pushes `a` *up*, which is the opposite of what the `K·spread` shade does.

When the item is worthless, `S(a) ≈ 0` and it collapses to `argmax a·G(a)` — no dependence on the item's value at all.

My belief representation differs too: a 5-knot ladder `q10…q90` interpolated in `log(price)` with lognormal tails, under a hurdle model — `t = 0` with probability `1 − p_valid`, else drawn from the positive part — so `S(a) = p_valid · (1 − F₊(a))`.

## 4. What is fitted, and what is guessed

| quantity | status |
|---|---|
| `B_QUANTILE = 1/3` | **derived** from the payoff table |
| `t_low/t_mid/t_high` | LLM ensemble median |
| `K = 0.5` | **hand-set**, and the data says it's wrong (5 of 8 measurable items had `t > t_mid`) |
| `UNCOVERED_CHARGE = 0.6` | **hand-set**, and provably the wrong functional form — the value it scales by doesn't enter the objective |
| `mu_shift`, `sigma_scale` | exist in my models, currently 1.0, never fitted |
| `G(a)` | measured offline; not wired into pricing |

So the honest summary: **`b` is a theorem and it's working. `t` is an LLM ensemble median. `a` is two hand-tuned constants, and both are the things currently costing money** — `K` at roughly 10,000/round, `UNCOVERED_CHARGE` at roughly 750/round.

`truth.py` already recovers the `t` intervals needed to fit `mu_shift` properly, and `feedback.py` already recovers the acceptance data needed to fit `G`. The missing piece is only the loop that closes them back into `price.py`.

Good — with `runs/` and `truth_game_*.json` local, the calibration loop has everything it needs. One fix first: my script mislabelled item 1 as "worthless". It isn't — `t ≥ 199.25` means it *is* covered. I'll treat it as undetermined below.

## The one hidden number

Each line has a secret ceiling `t`: the most a fair expert would sign off. Everything is a bet on which side of it your price sits.

## You play both sides, and they're lopsided in opposite directions

**As the handyman you cannot lose money.** Worst case, nobody pays you. There is no penalty for asking too much.

**As the insurer you cannot make money.** Best case, you pay the fair price.

So the whole game is: maximise collections, minimise leakage. They're separate problems.

## Why `b` is below your best guess

A charge arrives. You think there's a chance `p` it's genuinely owed.

- Pay it → costs `a`.
- Refuse it → if it *was* owed (chance `p`), you pay it anyway **plus half again** as a lawyer penalty. So refusing costs `1.5a × p` on average.

Refusing only wins when `1.5a·p < a`, i.e. **`p < 2/3`**.

Flip it round: *pay anything you're at least two-thirds sure is legitimate.* So `b` is the price where your confidence falls through 2/3 — and because you carry a *range* for `t`, that lands at the **⅓ point of the range**, noticeably below your best guess. Not timidity: the penalty is 1.5× and the alternative is 1×, so the asymmetry is 3:2 against refusing.

Game 4 says it's working: 240 reviews, **2 penalties totalling €79.50, and zero fraud funded.**

## Why `a` is a cliff, not a slope

This is the part that isn't obvious.

Charge **one euro under `t`** → *every* opponent pays you. All 16. Even the ones who refuse — they pay you anyway, plus their penalty.

Charge **one euro over `t`** → only reviewers whose own limit happens to sit above your price pay. In game 4 that was 2 to 7 out of 16.

So crossing `t` doesn't shave your income. It **divides it by two to eight.**

Game 4 makes it vivid:

| item | our `a` | payers | collected | |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | 532.50 | **16 / 16** | **8,520** | just under `t` — 55% of our income from one line |
| 2 | 335.00 | 4 / 16 | 1,340 | but `t ≥ 229.50`, so ~230 would have paid **3,672** |

**That single overcharge on item 2 cost about €2,300.**

## So when is charging over `t` right?

Compare the two plays: `16 × (just under t)` versus `your price × payers`. Rearranged, the safe play wins whenever

```
t  >  a × payers / 16
```

- **Item 2**: `335 × 4/16 = 84`. `t` is at least 229 — far above 84. Safe play wins clearly. We got this wrong.
- **Items 5–15**: `t = 0`. Nothing is owed at all, so there *is* no safe play. Every charge is a free lottery ticket, and they paid **€1,690** across 11 lines at zero risk.
- **Item 1**: break-even 232, and `t ∈ [199, 530)`. Genuinely undetermined — could have gone either way.

So the two cases need **opposite** behaviour, and telling them apart *is* the coverage question. That's why `b` collapsing to zero and `a` staying positive on the same line isn't a contradiction — it's the correct response to "worth nothing to me, still worth asking".

## Refinement of what I told you last turn

I said push free shots higher because the acceptance curve looked flat. Game 4 sharpens that: **true only when `t` is actually zero.** On items 1 and 2 — genuinely covered — pushing high cost us money. The lever isn't "how high", it's "is `t` zero or not".

## Where the 9,015 came from

```
income   15,500  =  8,760 fair (items 3, 4)  +  6,740 free shots
cost      6,485  =  6,405 legitimate claims paid  +  79.50 penalties
net       9,015
```

Headroom: placing `a` at the *proven* `t` on every line would have earned **18,040 instead of 15,500** — +2,540, almost all of it item 2, plus item 4 where we charged 15 against `t ≥ 28` (the `K` shading undercharging again).

Two things to tweak, both now measurable from the files you pulled down: stop overcharging covered lines (that's `K`), and stop undercharging the confident ones (also `K`, opposite direction — which is the argument for *fitting* it rather than picking a constant).
